newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn tries to resuscitate tax reforms.
newsitem.headline: Bonn tries to resuscitate tax reforms.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl won a parliamentary vote on Tuesday to revive coalition tax reforms, but the opposition vowed to kill off the plan and pressed for early general elections.
Deputies from Kohl's three-party alliance voted in the Bundestag lower house to overturn a decision by parliament's mediation committee to reject 30 billion marks in tax cuts.

The vote opens the way for a second round of mediation this autumn but the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) -- who control both the upper house and the mediation committee -- said they would just veto the plans again.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel accused the SPD of blocking urgent reforms for party-political reasons, and said compromise was vital to fix Germany's failing tax system.
"You have sacrificed the common good on the altar of party tactics," he told deputies in a speech.
Waigel attacked SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine for vetoing his tax plans, while promising that the SPD would introduce its own reforms if it won general elections in September 1998.
"That is an evil strategy. We need the reforms for jobs, investment and the economy," Waigel said. "We need a reform to prevent further erosion and put tax revenues on a sound basis."
Waigel was speaking after the Ifo economic think-tank said federal and state tax revenues would this year fall short of official targets revised sharply downwards in May.

Ifo also revised its forecast for the budget deficit up to 3.3 percent of gross domestic product. That is above Waigel's goal of exactly three percent but not too high, Ifo said, to prevent Germany from joining Europe's single currency in 1999 on a broad interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.

Politicians had earlier basked in the unity which helped the government team up with the SPD-led state of Brandenburg in the successful battle against the threat of flooding from the brimming Oder River in eastern Germany.
But they relapsed into bickering over who was to blame for the breakdown of efforts at tax reforms.

SPD tax negotiator Henning Voscherau dismissed accusations his party was pursuing a tactical blockade. He said the SPD also wanted a tax reform -- but only one which was affordable and which would ease the burden on workers and families.
"There is no blockade strategy -- there are just different views and opposing concepts," Voscherau, who is also mayor of the northern city of Hamburg, told deputies.
Speakers from minority parties dismissed the debate -- called in the Bundestag's summer recess -- as a waste of time.

"Anyone following this debate will have realised that the only sensible things were said about the flooding on the Oder -- the rest was a pure election campaign show," Greens finance spokeswoman Kerstin Mueller said.
Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS) leader Gregor Gysi, supported SPD calls for Kohl to quit: "Don't postpone your defeat. Give us all a chance. Call early elections," he said.

The Bundestag also passed a cross-party compromise reached in the mediation committee to scrap a capital trading tax on companies. But Kohl's majority voted down an SPD proposal designed to create jobs by cutting jobs insurance charges.

Earlier, the Kohl coalition managed to settle a potentially divisive internal row over cutting an income tax surcharge next year -- whether or not Waigel's main tax reform survives. It also agreed to bring forward pensions reforms to 1998.
Coalition leaders said Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) had bowed to calls by junior partners the Free Democrats (FDP) to cut the solidarity surcharge by two points to 5.5 percent.
